אִירוּס נַצְרָתִי או אִירִיס נַצְרָתִי (: The Nazareth iris (Hebrew: Irus Natzrati or Iris Natzrati; scientific name: Iris bismarckiana) is a species in the Oncocyclus section (the royal irises), in the subgenus Iris of the genus Iris. The Nazareth iris is endemic to northern Israel, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. In Israel the species grows in the Nazareth Hills, on Givat HaMoreh, in the Naftali Hills and at the foot of Mount Hermon. East of the Jordan River, the Nazareth iris grows in the Gilead region of Jordan. Because Muslims customarily plant it in cemeteries, it is assumed that certain populations were brought to their locations by humans. Several populations growing in the wild probably developed from plants that were planted in Muslim cemeteries.

Nabi Hazuri (Arabic: مقام النبي الحزوري, مقام سيّدنا الحزّوري, مقام الحزوري) is the burial site of the Druze holy man Sheikh Othman Hazuri, located in the northern Golan Heights about a kilometer east of Nimrod Fortress (Qal'at Namrud). At the site is an ancient oak grove, which became sanctified following the sanctity of the tomb. The tomb structure from the period of Syrian rule had a white cone-shaped dome. In recent decades the structure has been expanded.
The site also holds a memorial to the fallen of the Egoz reconnaissance unit in its various incarnations, with thirty-one memorial corners in memory of the unit's thirty-one fallen. Also commemorated at the site is Nachman Alexandron, one of the heads of the Jewish National Fund, who planned the site before his death.

Nahal Meron is one of the tributaries of Nahal Amud, located in the Upper Galilee. The stream flows eastward from the slopes of Mount Meron, passing through agricultural land and many natural areas, and empties into Nahal Amud. The stream is about 5 kilometers long and is considered relatively short, but of great historical and geographical importance. The stream's course passes near Moshav Meron and north of Har Mesarvim. Along it are several springs, including Ein Meron ("Mei Megiddo") and Ein Bar-Yochai.
Up on the northern bank, near Moshav Meron, are the ancient synagogue of Meron and the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. On the southern bank are the remains of the synagogue at Horvat Shema.

Nahal Taninim (Arabic: وَادِي ٱلزَّرْقَاءِ - Wadi az-Zarqa, "the Blue Stream") is a perennial stream that begins in the Menashe Heights (Ramot Menashe) between the kibbutzim Dalia and Ein HaShofet. The stream flows southwest and empties into the Mediterranean Sea right beside Jisr az-Zarqa and south of Kibbutz Ma'agan Michael. Other, older names for the stream are "Crocodilon" and "Tamasih".
Near Moshav Aviel, the Mekorot water company built a dam across the channel of Nahal Taninim as part of the "Menashe Streams" project. On winter days when the flow in the stream is strong, the stream's water (together with water from the Ada, Barkan and Mishmarot streams) is diverted into a canal that carries the water to an infiltration reservoir for groundwater recharge in the Caesarea dunes.
עמק האלה הוא עמק קטן בשפלת יהודה, מדרום:
The Elah Valley (Emek HaEla) is a small valley in the Judean Lowlands (Shephelah), south of Beit Shemesh, known as the site of the battle between David and Goliath as recounted in the Bible. The Elah Valley is considered one of the most fertile areas in the Land of Israel, and it links the Shephelah with the Judean Hills and the Adullam region, hence its importance over the years. To this day a large number of archaeological sites and biblical tells stand out in the valley and its surroundings.
At the beginning of 2014 a plan to declare the Elah Valley a national park was deposited, and in July 2019 it was declared a national park and passed to the management of the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, mainly because of its historical importance and the desire to limit the southward expansion of Beit Shemesh's urban area into the valley.
דרך נוף יער בית קשת היא דרך נופית בגליל:
The Beit Keshet Forest Scenic Road is a scenic road in the Lower Galilee. It is named after Kibbutz Beit Keshet, which the road passes beside. The northern entrance to the road is next to Camp Shimshon; the entrance is from Route 77, about 2 km west of the Golani Interchange. The road passes by Beit Keshet, next to which is the eastern entrance, reached from Route 65. From there the road turns southwest toward Nof HaGalil.
The southern entrance to the road is near Har Ksulot and Churchill Forest. An additional scenic road section circles Kibbutz Beit Keshet. It begins at the eastern entrance near Tel Govel, turns toward Mount Deborah (Har Dvora), and after several kilometers the road turns south toward Nahal HaShiv'a and returns to the eastern entrance.

Nahal Shiloh is an ephemeral stream in the Binyamin region, one of the main tributaries of the Yarkon River. The stream drains 400 square kilometers, which is about 22% of the Yarkon River's drainage basin (1,805 square kilometers).
Nahal Shiloh begins in the east of the Shiloh Valley and flows west, north of El'ad, until it joins the Yarkon River about three kilometers east of the Morasha Interchange. It reaches a length of about 50 kilometers, and alongside it lie impressive heritage, nature and landscape sites, including Nehushonim Forest, Kula Forest, Migdal Afek and Deir Qal'a.
Shmuel Safrai and Amit Shadman hold that in the Second Temple period Nahal Shiloh was a natural border between areas settled by Jews (to the south) and areas settled by Samaritans (to the north).

Nahal Oren (Arabic: Wadi Fallah) is a stream that flows in Mount Carmel. It begins at an elevation of 420 meters above sea level, near the central watershed line of the Carmel in the area of "Horvat Ma'atzera", about two kilometers south-southeast of Isfiya. It is about 14 km long and empties into the Mediterranean Sea north of Atlit. Nahal Oren is the largest of the western drainage basins of the Carmel. Its drainage basin covers about 35 square kilometers. Route 721, which leads from Route 4 to Route 672, runs along the lower western part of the stream's channel.
The stream's drainage basin is composed mainly of rocks from the Cenomanian-Turonian period such as limestone, dolomite and chalk, as well as several tuff outcrops. Most sections of the stream are characterized by a narrow, deep channel.

Mashhad (Persian: Ⓘ, literally "place of martyrdom", related to the Arabic word "shahid") is the second-largest city in Iran and the capital of Razavi Khorasan Province in the northeast of the country. The city is located about 736 km east of the capital Tehran and about 210 km southeast of Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan. Its elevation is 995 meters above sea level.
The city is holy to Shia Muslims because of the Imam Reza Shrine, where the tomb of the eighth Imam, Ali al-Rida, is located (in Persian his name is often pronounced Emam Reza). Millions of Shia believers visit the tomb every year. The city is also known as the city of Ferdowsi, the Iranian poet who wrote the Shahnameh, considered the national epic of Iran, whose tomb is located near the city.

Bar'am National Park is a national park containing a synagogue from the Talmudic period, whose remains are among the most beautiful built in that era and attest to the existence of a well-established Jewish community at the site. The park extends over a hilltop 755 meters above sea level, overlooking the surrounding area. Kfar Bar'am, the name of the Jewish settlement in which the synagogue stands, is first mentioned in 1210 by the traveler Rabbi Shmuel bar Shimshon, and it apparently came to an end in the Mamluk period.
Within the national park are the buildings of the Arab village of Bir'im, whose residents, Maronite Christians, were evacuated from it during the War of Independence and were not allowed to return afterwards, despite the promises they had received. Over the years the displaced people of Iqrit and Bir'im have waged a legal struggle in the state's institutions demanding to return to their village.
נְתַנְיָה היא עיר במחוז המרכז בישראל, הש:
Netanya is a city in Israel's Central District, the seventh most populous city in the State of Israel. The place was founded by the Bnei Binyamin group in 1929 as a settlement for the sons of the moshavot and for citrus grove workers, and was declared a city in 1948. Netanya is also called the "Capital of the Sharon", because it is the largest city in the Sharon region, and the "Diamond City", because of the developed diamond industry that once existed there.
The city lies on the coastal plain (Central District) on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, on kurkar (calcareous sandstone) ground. The seashore is characterized by high kurkar cliffs along the city's entire coastline, except for its southernmost part – the Poleg neighborhood and Ir Yamim.
The city is named after the philanthropist Nathan Straus, and it is the largest city in Israel whose name commemorates a person.
בקעת קנאים היא בקעה בשולי מדבר יהודה הדר:
Bik'at Kana'im (the Zealots' Valley) is a valley on the southern edge of the Judean Desert, 309 meters above sea level. It is bounded on the east by Har Kana'im, on the west by Har Tzfira, and on the south by Har Menachem. North of it is Nahal Tze'elim, a deep wadi that drops hundreds of meters below the level of the valley; in the section adjacent to the valley lies Birkat Tzfira, which is reached through the valley. It is named after the Zealots who were active during the Great Revolt against the Roman Empire and operated in this area.
In the valley is Kfar HaNokdim, a major holiday village in the area.
Route 3199 crosses the valley in an east–west direction, in its section between Arad and Masada. From it, an unpaved road 3.5 km long branches off along the center of the valley. The Israel National Trail in this section runs between Arad and Masada.

Nahal Bokek (Arabic: وادي البغق or بقق or المقلق) is a stream in the Judean Desert about 15 km long, with a catchment area of about 21 square kilometers. The stream descends from Har Ben Nesher and empties onto the shore of the Dead Sea. South of the stream is Nahal Zohar and north of it Nahal Ye'elim. The Dead Sea hotels and the Ein Bokek baths were built on its large alluvial fan. North of the stream's channel, near where it empties into the Dead Sea, stands the Byzantine fortress of Metzad Bokek.
For most of its course the stream runs across the desert plateau, cutting into soft rock (chalk and the Hatrurim Formation), so its valley is shallow. Within the fault escarpment, the stream passes two waterfalls, the first about 100 meters high and the second about 60. After the first waterfall the stream continues flowing through a short (about 1.5 km) deep canyon.
מטע היא יחידת ייצור חקלאית המאופיינת, לר:
A plantation (orchard) is an agricultural production unit characterized, as a rule, by a single agricultural crop. 
Plantations grow various crops such as cotton, tobacco, coffee, sugar cane or fruit trees. Nevertheless, the use of the term "plantation" (mata) is today mainly characteristic of descriptions of tree plantations and orchards.
A plantation is a planned and systematic form of agricultural activity intended to achieve large yields while ensuring optimal use of the land resource and of other inputs such as water, fertilizer, labor, pest control and protection against other threats. Planting is done in rows and columns, which eases the stages of planting, irrigation, care and harvesting. 
In the last generation a method of protection using nets has become common, to reduce damage from birds  and strong wind. In this respect the plantation method is approaching the greenhouse method.

Makhtesh Yeruham (HaGadol; formerly the Large Crater / Makhtesh Hatira) is an erosional crater (makhtesh) located in the eastern Negev in Israel, and one of the five makhteshim of the Negev—similar craters in the region that formed in a similar way, a unique phenomenon that is rare in the world and exists mainly in this area. The makhtesh is elliptical in shape and is the second largest of the Negev makhteshim. It is located in the Hatira anticline, hence its other name.
The makhtesh is 14 km long and 6 km wide. Its maximum depth is 410 meters. The stream that drains it is Nahal Hatira. The makhtesh's boundaries are the Hatira ridge in the west and the Har Karbolet ridge in the east and south, along which the Israel National Trail runs. Northwest of the Large Crater is Har Avnon, rising to a height of 656 meters, from which there is a fine view over the makhtesh.

Neve Ativ is a moshav of the HaIhud HaHakla'i movement on the slopes of Mount Hermon, at an elevation of 950 to 1,050 meters above sea level, about 2 kilometers southwest of Majdal Shams and about 17 kilometers northeast of Kiryat Shmona. It is the third-northernmost settlement in Israel, after Metula and Majdal Shams, and the northernmost settlement in the Golan Regional Council. Route 989 passes through the moshav, where it is called "Sayeret Egoz Boulevard".
The settlement's name is an acronym of the names of four fighters of the Egoz reconnaissance unit who were killed in the course of their military service in the northern Golan Heights: Avraham HaMeiri, Tuvia Sherkinger, Yair Algranti (killed in a military operation near the Oil Road in the Golan on 3 September 1968) and Binyamin Hadad (killed in an ambush near Yardena on 30 April 1968).
עין כרם (בערבית: عين كارم; ההגייה הרשמית: Ein Karem (Arabic: عين كارم; the official pronunciation of the Hebrew name is Ein Kerem, but the common pronunciation is Ein Karem, following the Arabic) is a neighborhood on the southwestern outskirts of Jerusalem. The site was inhabited as early as the Canaanite period; from the 14th century until the War of Independence an Arab village stood there, which was abandoned during the war. New immigrants were settled in the empty houses, and as part of Jerusalem's expansion the village was declared a neighborhood of the city. Even today the neighborhood retains a rural character, owing to its relative separation from the city and its being surrounded by hills, valleys and forests. Ein Karem is also considered a place sacred to Christianity and a pilgrimage site, being known as the birthplace of John the Baptist; there are several churches and monasteries there, visited by many tourists.

The Hatira Ridge or Hatira Anticline is a mountain ridge in the eastern Negev, one of six parallel anticlines in this region whose general orientation is from southwest to northeast, and the highest of them (its peak at 704 meters above sea level). Southeast of the Hatira Ridge is the Oron-Yamin syncline, and northwest of it the Dimona–Yeruham–Sde Boker road (Route 204).
In the Hatira Ridge lies the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol), which is an erosional crater. Near the ridge's highest point, at the southwestern end of the makhtesh, there is a monument in memory of Avraham Krinitzi, mayor of Ramat Gan in the 1960s (the road leading from the makhtesh to the monument and the lookout beside it was broken through by the Paratroopers Brigade in 1964, and they named it "Ma'ale Avraham" after Krinitzi, whose city had adopted the paratroopers).

Yardenit is a baptismal site on the Jordan River intended for Christian pilgrims. The site is located south of the river's outlet from the Sea of Galilee, between the Degania Dam and the Alumot Dam near Kvutzat Kinneret, and is owned by the kvutza. The site has 12 separate baptismal pools. In 2012 the site's capacity was doubled in light of the large number of visitors.
According to Christian tradition, John the Baptist baptized Jesus at Qasr al-Yahud, north of the Dead Sea and east of Jericho. For hundreds of years Qasr al-Yahud was an important site for pilgrim visits, and monasteries and hostels were built near it. After the Six-Day War, Qasr al-Yahud became a frontier zone on the border between Israel and Jordan. As a substitute for that site, after the area was declared a closed military zone during the War of Attrition, the Ministry of Tourism initiated the establishment of Yardenit in 1981.
עין ירקעם הוא מעיין עונתי הנובע בחלק העל:
Ein Yorke'am is a seasonal spring that emerges in the upper part of Nahal Hatira, east of the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol). The spring flows mainly in winter. In this season the groundwater level rises above ground level (a "tamila"). Usually its waters are also flooded by rainwater and flash floods, filling a large rock pool (gev) to a depth of up to 5 meters. Toward the end of summer little water remains, only in the lower part of the pool, while its upper part dries out, but the spring's groundwater remains relatively high and the animals of the area manage to reach it with a little digging in the sand. The spring is surrounded by abundant vegetation, mainly reeds and tamarisk.
Ancient steps are carved into the wall of the stream's northern bank, which apparently served to bring camels down to drink from the pool. Near the spring is Metzad Yorke'am, a fortress from the Byzantine period that served as a security post.
מאוזוליאום מזור הוא מאוזוליאום רומי מאמצ:
The Mazor Mausoleum is a Roman mausoleum from the mid-3rd century, situated on the western outskirts of the city of El'ad, east of Route 444 and Route 6. The structure stands at an elevation of about 75 meters above sea level, on the northern side of Nahal Mazor. The site on which the structure stands was declared a national park on 21 March 2002 and covers about 25 dunams.
This structure is the only one of its kind in the Land of Israel west of the Jordan to have survived intact from the Roman period. The structure was preserved because for a long period it served as a Muslim place of prayer known as "Maqam an-Nabi Yahya". The structure, 4.8 meters high, is built as a square chamber containing the remains of sarcophagi apparently intended for a married couple. Its ceiling is made of ashlar slabs carried on two arches. Its thick walls and small windows maintain a constant temperature inside.
עמודי עמרם הם עמודים העשויים אבן חול נוב:
Amram's Pillars (Amudei Amram) are pillars made of soft, colorful Nubian sandstone in a pink hue, standing on a cliff at the start of Nahal Amram, at the point where it begins its course toward the Arava. The stream flows in the Eilat Mountains north of Eilat.
The pillars were formed by rainwater cutting into cracks that existed in the cliff. Erosion of the rock along the cracks produced weathering and led to the formation of five tall pillars rising to a height of 15 meters. The hill next to the pillars is called "Givat Yocheved", after Yocheved, the mother of Moses and wife of Amram. The area in which the pillars stand is part of the Eilat Massif Nature Reserve.
The sandstone from which the pillars were formed was created by the weathering of basement rock. The colors that appear in the sandstone are the result of its being washed by water rich in oxides of various materials such as iron, manganese and others.

Mount Meron (Arabic: جبل الجرمق, Jabal al-Jarmaq) is the highest mountain in the Land of Israel west of the Jordan River and the fourth highest in Israel as a whole. It lies between Safed and Ma'alot-Tarshiha, and its summit rises to 1,204 meters above sea level, the highest point in the Meron range of the Upper Galilee. In the past the mountain rose to 1,208 meters above sea level, but the IDF flattened the summit in order to build an air control unit and lowered it slightly.
Mount Meron is one of the rainiest areas in Israel, receiving on average about 900 millimeters of rain a year. In most winters snow falls on Mount Meron and accumulates. The mountain is covered in Mediterranean maquis that includes oak shrubs, carob, red-trunked strawberry trees (Arbutus andrachne) and others.
Following the Swords of Iron War, before Lag BaOmer the mountain was declared a closed military zone.
תל עזקה (זכריה) הייתה עיר קדומה בליבה של: Tel Azekah (Tell Zakariya) was an ancient city in the heart of the Judean Lowlands (Shephelah). The upper tell is located 347 m above sea level and 117 m above the channel of Nahal HaEla, and its area is about 45 dunams. The tell is located in Britannia Park, managed by KKL-JNF. The site lies at the northern end of a north–south ridge that forms the boundary between the high Shephelah to the east and the low Shephelah to the west. Azekah commands the strategic junction of the road leading from Philistine Gath through the Elah Valley toward the Judean Hills to the east with the road linking Beit Shemesh in the north and Lachish in the south; for these reasons Azekah naturally became an important city. Excavations at the site uncovered remains of settlement mainly from the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age II, a fortress, towers, LMLK seal impressions and other finds. In addition, hiding caves from the period of the Bar Kokhba revolt were discovered at the site.

Mount Shlomo (Har Shlomo), 705 meters high, is one of the oldest mountains in the Eilat Mountains range. Its age is estimated at hundreds of millions of years more than most of the mountains surrounding it. It is about 500 million years older than the adjacent Mount Yehoram.
The mountain is named after King Solomon, who established the mines in the area. Mount Shlomo was meant to be the highest of the mountains named after one of the kings of Judah, but King Hezekiah had a mountain higher than Solomon's named after him, because in Hezekiah's days the Kingdom of Judah's control over this area was restored, after a prolonged revolt by the Edomites.
The mountain is made of magmatic and metamorphic rocks, hence its black color.
The mountain's summit is connected by marked trails to Mount Yehoram, Nahal Shlomo and Route 12, as well as to Nahal Netafim. The marked trails on Mount Shlomo are characterized by especially steep gradients, due to the mountain's overall structure.

Tzova or Palmach Tzova (formerly also called "Tzuba") is a collective kibbutz located in the Jerusalem Corridor, near Mevaseret Zion. The kibbutz sits on a mountain spur 735 meters above sea level, and beside it is Tel Tzova, 769 meters high. The village of Suba, on whose ruins the kibbutz was built, as well as the kibbutz's name, preserve the name of the biblical settlement Zobah, whose remains lie at Tel Tzova.
The kibbutz's economic branches are: industry (the "Oran" factory for automotive safety glass and bullet-resistant glass), and agriculture (including orchards, vineyards, irrigated field crops, olives, tomatoes and hydroponic cabbage grown on water).
In the kibbutz and its surroundings there are many attractions, such as Ein Tzova and its 50-meter-long tunnel, and the Cave of John the Baptist. The kibbutz's tourism branch includes the "Kiftzuba" amusement park for children and the "Tzuba" country hotel. The kibbutz also has a Hebrew-language ulpan.
חוות כנרת (או חצר כנרת) היא חווה חקלאית:
Kinneret Farm (Havat Kinneret, or Kinneret Courtyard) is an agricultural farm established in 1908 on the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It was founded by the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization, at the suggestion of its director, Arthur Ruppin, in order to train Jewish workers in agricultural work and construction for the sake of permanent settlement.
The farm's graduates became the thinkers and founders of the diverse settlement enterprises of the Second Aliyah period and the labor movement: it was here that the first attempts to establish the kvutza, the kibbutz and the moshav began (the settlers of Degania, Kvutzat Kinneret, Nahalal, Ein Harod and others came from it), it became a center of organization for the country's workers, and here the foundations were laid for several organizations that shaped the face of the state-in-the-making, such as the Haganah, HaMashbir, Tnuva and Solel Boneh.
The site was recognized as a heritage site by the Council for Conservation of Heritage Sites in Israel and by the Landmarks (Tzionei Derech) program.
בית גוברין - מָרֵשָׁה הוא גן לאומי שהוכר:
Beit Guvrin-Maresha is a national park declared in 1989 in order to preserve the remains of the city of Maresha, to continue research at the site and to conserve the natural woodland. The national park extends over an area of 5,000 dunams and contains many caves, a variety of underground chambers and important archaeological remains. In the southern and highest part of the park is Tel Maresha.
The bedrock of the Judean Lowlands consists of a layer of chalk, a soft limestone mainly from the Eocene epoch, deposited in an ancient sea. Above the chalk developed a layer 1–3 meters thick of hard limestone known as 'nari'. The chalk bedrock is convenient for quarrying underground chambers and for producing building blocks. Most of the building blocks were quarried from bell-shaped caves with a round opening at the top. Through these openings the quarrymen began their work, quarrying downward row after row and hauling the chalk blocks up for construction purposes.
תֵּל עֲרָד הוא אתר ארכאולוגי בבקעת ערד,:
Tel Arad is an archaeological site in the Arad Valley, about 8 km west of the city of Arad. The tell stands at an elevation of 576 meters above sea level. Tel Arad lies at an important crossroads from the Early Bronze Age to the present day. In the Iron Age, Arad guarded the main road that ran from Jerusalem, Hebron and the Arad Valley toward Horvat Uza and the Dead Sea. Yohanan Aharoni identifies this road with the route of the Way of the Land of Edom (Derekh Eretz Edom).
The tell has two main parts: a large city from the Early Bronze Age, whose remains were visible on the surface even before excavations began; and a fortress on the top of the hill included within this city, dating to Iron Age II (the period of the Monarchy).
Excavations were conducted at the site over 18 seasons, 14 of them in the Early Bronze Age city, headed by Ruth Amiran. A first expedition worked at the site in the years 1962–1966, and the second between 1971 and 1980.

Nahal Peres (Arabic: Wadi Faresh) is an ephemeral stream in the northeastern Negev. It is about 17 km long and flows southeast, parallel to and north of Ma'ale Tamar (Route 25). It begins in Bik'at Tzva'im, about 3 km east of Tzafit Junction, and at its end it empties into Nahal Tamar, about a kilometer and a half east of the Arava Junction.
It is commonly thought that the stream is named after the bird of prey peres (the bearded vulture), but the source of its name is the word "faresh" or "al-faresh" in Arabic, meaning a carpet, mattress or bed, it being a spread-out, enclosed valley suited to camel grazing. The stream is also an ancient Roman road that linked Rafah with the biblical city of Zoar.
In its eastern part the stream flows through a canyon containing rock pools (gevim). In the Ma'ale Peres area, before the confluence with Nahal Tamar, there is a high waterfall of about 50 meters.
Nahal Peres has one tributary – Nahal Tahmas, which originates at Metzad Tamar and meets it at the foot of Har Tzurim.

Jisr az-Zarqa (Arabic: جسر الزرقاء, exact transliteration: Jisr al-Zarqa', sometimes called Jisr for short; in translation: the Blue Bridge) is a local council in the Haifa District of Israel. The village was founded in 1924 and declared a local council in 1961. All the residents of Jisr az-Zarqa are Muslim Arabs.
The town sits on a strip of kurkar (calcareous sandstone) on the Mediterranean coast, 5–20 meters above sea level, at whose foot flows the lower section of Nahal Taninim, which separates the town from the sea to the west. To the south lies Caesarea, and to the north Ma'agan Michael and the entrance to the Nahal Taninim Nature Reserve. To the east the town borders Route 2 (the Haifa–Tel Aviv highway). Near the stream's mouth, southwest of the town's houses, lies Tel Taninim.
The name Jisr az-Zarqa means the Blue Bridge (over the stream), after the bridge built over Nahal Taninim, "al-Wadi az-Zarqa" (the Blue Stream in Arabic).

The Gulf of Eilat, known outside Israel as the Gulf of Aqaba (Arabic: خليج العقبة), is a long, narrow inlet, a northern arm of the Red Sea separating the Sinai Peninsula from the Arabian Peninsula. The gulf is about 180 kilometers long and its maximum width is 25 kilometers. The gulf's area is 2,880 square kilometers, about 0.5% of the area of the entire Red Sea. The gulf's volume is 2,500 cubic kilometers, about 1% of the volume of the entire Red Sea. Its average depth is 900 meters below sea level and its maximum depth is 1,820 meters below sea level (in the area opposite Nuweiba, near the Saudi coast). Geologically, the Gulf of Eilat is part of the Syrian-African Rift, hence its great depth.
Steep mountains rise on both sides of the Gulf of Eilat – the Sinai mountains to the west and the mountains of Edom and Midian to the east. The average gradient of the gulf floor is 21%, and in certain sections the slope exceeds 50%.
עין לימון, כנראה שיבוש של השם עין לימור,:
Ein Limon, probably a corruption of the name Ein Limor, which is itself a corruption of the name Ein al-Umur (after the village of Khirbet al-Umur that stood nearby), is a layer spring in Nahal Kisalon in the Jerusalem Hills, about a kilometer west of Ein Rafa, at the foot of Har Tzova. On the PEF map and on the 1948 map of the Survey of Israel (the Center for Mapping of the Land of Israel), the spring is called "Ein Mahtush".
Before the War of Independence a village, Khirbet al-Umur, stood at the site, and the pool served its residents. The village sat on a hill about 700 meters west of the spring.
At the site is a small square concrete pool located inside a quarried cutting measuring 18X10 meters, which apparently was the pool in the past. The pool receives its water through a 15-meter-long tunnel that carries the spring water to it. The tunnel and pool are dated to the Roman period in the Land of Israel.
The spring lies on the Israel National Trail, and many hikers tend to stop there to bathe and rest (and some also spend the night at its foot).

Nahal Tzipori is a perennial stream flowing from the Nazareth Hills to the Kishon River. The stream, 32 km long, begins its course at the town of Reineh, passes through the hills of Alonim Forest near Shefa-'Amr, and drains into the Kishon River (which in turn drains into Haifa Bay on the Mediterranean coast). It is fed by Einot Tzipori, Einot Yiftah'el and Ein Yivka, and by a large number of intermittent springs such as Ein Rani, Ein Avinoam, Ein Mahil, Ein Gat Hefer, Ein Amat Avel, Ein Lapidot and Ein Tur'an. On old maps such as the Jacotin maps of 1799 and the PEF maps the stream is called Nahar wadi melik, after the wadi in which it flows. Today the name Wadi Milek is attributed to a different wadi. The stream empties into the Kishon near the Bazan (oil refineries) complex.
There is evidence of settlement at the site from thousands of years ago, and along the stream are flour mills and the remains of ancient settlements. Several Bedouin tribes live along the stream in the villages of Zarzir, Ka'abiyye-Tabbash-Hajajre, Khawaled and Hilf.
הר דבורה (בערבית: جبل سرطبة; ג'בל סָרְטָ:
Mount Deborah (Har Dvora; Arabic: جبل سرطبة, Jabal Sartaba) is a mountain in Israel 437 meters above sea level, located in the Nazareth Hills of the Lower Galilee, on the edge of the Jezreel Valley to its south. It lies between Har Ksulot to the west, Har Yona to the north and Mount Tabor, which is 4.5 km to its southeast. On the mountain's eastern slopes lies the village of Daburiyya, to its west the city of Nof HaGalil, and in the valley to its north the village of Ein Mahil. The mountain's name commemorates the prophetess Deborah, who defeated Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor, in battle in the valley at its foot.
The mountain is made of limestone and dolomite, and its soil is terra rossa. It is wooded with Mediterranean maquis, especially oak trees. The site was declared a forest reserve as early as the British Mandate period, in 1926, and was called "Sartaba Forest". On the summit KKL-JNF prepared a picnic area, and there stands a rock commemorating the 25th wedding anniversary of Queen Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom and Prince Philip, celebrated in 1972.
